new_statements.quote: LSC uses different prosodic manual and non-manual strategies in order to mark focused elements. [...] 4.3.1. Focus. Prosodic manual markers are used in LSC in the expression of focus. Focused signs are longer in duration, have a higher velocity of their movement and display more movement repetitions, than their unfocused counterparts. In the table below the sign APPLE is found in two different examples. In the first one, the sign is not focused and it is articulated in 461 ms. By contrast, in the second example, the sign APPLE is focused and its duration is longer: 575 ms.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Signed language: the only 'stress'/prominence the descriptions treat is sentence-level focus prominence, realized manually by longer duration, higher movement velocity and repetition of the focused sign (plus non-manuals functioning like intonation). No lexical word-stress (e.g. which syllable/movement of a disyllabic sign or compound is prominent) is described; the grammar's Prosody chapter (syllable, foot, prosodic word) is an empty placeholder.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the grammar notes noun-verb pairs differ mainly in duration (Morphology 2.1.2.1), which is derivational, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Phrase/sentence level (focus marking), measured on signs in elicited sentences; not citation-form word prosody. Variety described is Barcelona LSC (two native signers, Delfina Aliaga and Santiago Frigola).
new_statements.identity_note: cata1241 is a signed language (Llengua de signes catalana, LSC; ISO csc). The SIGN-HUB grammar describes the Barcelona variety (two native Deaf signers). 'Word stress' in the spoken-language sense is not applicable; the only prominence described is sentence-level focus marking. Not to be confused with spoken Catalan (stan1289).

new_statements.quote: Prosody in SLs is mainly marked by NMMs (as mentioned in § 2.4). Consequently, some NMMs are involved in the expression of focus. Nonetheless, focused signs are also marked by manual features, such as a longer duration of the sign, a larger movement trajectory, and a higher velocity of the movement, as mentioned earlier (§ 2.6). [p. 30] As mentioned above, some researchers argue that focused signs are stressed by having a larger duration, a higher velocity and a larger movement trajectory. This section mainly focuses in the manual realization of the sign, namely, it analyzes its duration, repetition and its localization in the manual signing space. [p. 31]
new_statements.citation: Navarrete-González, Alexandra. 2016. Focus constructions in Catalan Sign Language (LSC). MA thesis, Universitat Pompeu Fabra, Barcelona. 65 pp. hdl:10230/27671.

new_statements.relation_note: Same finding as the existing statement from the SIGN-HUB grammar (which cites this thesis as its source): focus prominence = longer duration, faster movement, more repetitions. Adds the measured durations, the repetition and signing-space markers, and the non-manual inventory. No word-level stress statement, so it neither confirms nor denies a lexical stress rule; the existing 'none found' reading for lexical stress stands.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only 'stress' the thesis describes is sentence-level focus prominence: a sign under (information, selective or corrective) focus is articulated longer (Table 3, p. 31: MAN 304-348 ms unfocused vs 428 ms information focus, 431 ms selective focus), with more movement repetitions and shifted use of signing space, plus non-manual markers (brows, mouthing, body leans, head movements). Nothing is said about prominence within a multi-syllabic sign or a fixed lexical stress position.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 31 caveat: focused fragments articulated in isolation get a following pause, which itself lengthens the sign, so the duration difference may be partly an artefact; velocity and trajectory length were not measured (left for future research).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Catalan Sign Language (LSC, llengua de signes catalana) as used by the Catalan Deaf community, elicited from Barcelona-area signers and the LSC corpus (Navarrete-González 2016, sec. 3.2 Participants); no dialect distinction is drawn.
